slots.title: Trump approves fuel rules ending Biden EV mandate
slots.body:
Trump posted Saturday that he approved new fuel-economy standards.

Reuters and CNBC report the move ends the Biden administration’s EV-linked mandate and reverses policies aimed at tighter fleet efficiency.

The story is policy, not a same-day economic print — it sets the frame for auto and energy regulation after the prior administration’s rules.

What part of the rollback — fleet averages, timelines, or state rules — do you think gets clarified first?

Headline: Trump says he approved new fuel economy standards rolling back Biden-era rules — source: FMP news / CNBC

slots.title: 10-year Treasury at 5.2% with 0.3% 2s–10s spread
slots.body:
The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield is 5.2% in the Sept. 24 Treasury snapshot in the data.

The 2-year is 4.9%.

The 2s–10s spread is 0.31 percentage point — the gap between short- and long-term government borrowing costs.

CNBC on Sept. 26 walks through how the 10-year reached its highest level in nearly two decades, citing sticky inflation, rate expectations, and heavy government and corporate bond supply.

On the Sept. 26 session close, the CBOE Volatility Index ($VIX) finished at 14.87, down 5.1% from the prior close.

Which matters more to you right now: the level of the 10-year or how much bond issuance is in the pipeline?

slots.title: Oil slips as Russia–Ukraine hits energy infrastructure
slots.body:
Brent crude settled at 104.32, down 2.1% on the session in the feed.

The United States Oil Fund ($USO) closed at 148.33, down 3.1%.

Both readings are prior-session closes, not live quotes.

Bloomberg This Weekend cites New York Times reporting that Russia and Ukraine are increasingly targeting each other’s economies, including energy and export infrastructure, as the conflict evolves.

That headline sits alongside the day’s oil price move — the data shows the move; the story names the geopolitical thread markets were reading.

Where do you look first when oil moves like this — inventory data, freight, or headlines out of the region?

slots.title: US close — Sept. 26, 2026
slots.body:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average led the U.S. index set, closing up 0.9% at 51,828.62, a 478.64-point gain on the session.

The S&P 500 finished up 0.5% at 7,743.41, and the Nasdaq Composite also rose 0.5% to 27,068.72.

The Russell 2000 barely moved, up 0.1% to 2,837.55, so the day’s strength skewed toward the large-cap benchmarks in the data.

The VIX fell 5.1% to 14.87, down 0.80 point from the prior close of 15.67.

Microsoft closed up 3.7% at 516.17, the largest percentage move among the injected megacaps; Apple rose 1.5% to 341.07, and Oracle slipped 1.8% to 137.08.

Intel, flagged among active names, closed down 3.4% at 123.00; NVIDIA edged up 0.2% to 225.07, and AMD added 0.2% to 630.63 with a year high in the file at 639.00.

ASML gained 1.2% to 1,743.94 in the equipment group, while Broadcom ticked up 0.7% to 352.81.

Energy equities and oil proxies weakened: Exxon Mobil fell 1.0% to 160.56, the USO oil fund closed down 3.1% at 148.33, and Brent crude was down 2.1% at 104.32 in the cross-asset block.

Gold futures rose 0.5% to 4,321.20; the dollar proxy UUP slipped 0.2% to 28.62, and bitcoin was roughly flat at 84,388.20 in the injected crypto quote.

The Treasury snapshot dated 2026-09-24 in the data showed the 10-year yield at 5.2% and the 2s10s spread at 0.31 percentage point.

Overseas indexes in the file were mixed: Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1.3% to 66,364.20, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1.3% to 24,510.10; the FTSE 100 added 0.1% to 10,695.25.

No sector ETF performance array was populated in this payload, and the earnings calendar block was empty for the session.

Headlines in the feed included Trump’s statement on new fuel-economy standards and weekend pieces on Treasury yields and chip demand; those stories sat alongside the price moves above rather than replacing them.
